notes:
The tail of the archive, read as one batch: **36 collections holding between one and nineteen addressed records each**, 7,261 catalogue records in all. Everything left after the twelve collections read on their own, minus SFP 130, SFP 179 and SFP 136, which are blocked on #217. Reading them one at a time would have been 36 findings files, 36 register lines and 36 dossier entries for 188 candidate addresses, so `digitalsf_extract.py` now takes a comma-separated list of collections and resolves the description template and the three policies per record.

**All 36 take the same two policies**, both conservative. `skip-unnumbered`, because the unnumbered majority of every one is portraits, parades, streetcars and street corners — 6,185 of the 7,261 records. And `named-buildings-only`, because these are caption collections and the captions are about people: bar customers, marchers, volunteers, a mayor at a party, a photographer's own household. The strict filter kept 13 firm names and dropped 164 fragments, and it dropped real businesses with them — Maud's, Amelia's, Castro Camera, the Coffee Gallery, Club Q. That trade is only affordable because the batch is small enough to read by eye: where the record plainly names a business rather than a person, the name was put back by hand at publication, one page at a time.

**They also take `drop` for the archivist's notes**, which is the change this batch forced. In these collections `500$a` is not housekeeping — it is a donor's memoir, a police case note or a newspaper's copy, and it names people: a robbery victim with her home apartment number, the children at a blackboard, a donor's parents and their hotel, the party to a 1941 collision and his street address. None of it can ever become a page fact and `citation.url` is one click from the record, so it does not enter the repository at all.

**The widened year guard removed 28 candidates before they became findings.** A street number equal to the record's own year was already refused, but `year_of` returns the archivist's whole phrase for an imprecise date — "not before 1906" — which equals no street number ever, so the guard missed exactly the captions that name the year in words. It now compares against every four-digit year the date carries. Measured over every findings file in the repository first: it changes nothing already committed.

**31 rejections were made by hand**, in two groups. Twenty-four are numbers that were never addresses and that no guard should be widened to catch — a car's model year, a Muni route, a baseball season, a regiment, a postcard's own catalogue number, a Navy quarters number. Four are outside San Francisco. Four are Dupont Street, and those are the ones worth reading: **Dupont is today's Grant Avenue and the numbers do carry over, but the buildings do not.** EAS holds no 1011, 1013, 1017 or 714 Grant Avenue today. The album is the Board of Health photographing Chinatown facades in 1903, the year its own campaign demolished 160 buildings there, and the 1906 fire took the rest.

**A page's own description drops the address**, because the page is the address: the finding reads "Photographed at 1345 Montgomery Street in 1959" and the timeline row reads "Leslie Sheraton photographed the property, showing Shadows Restaurant." That is the shape the digitalsf rows already on pages use.

The densest thing in the tail is **SFH 611, the Junior League of San Francisco's Here Today building research files**: ten records, ten addresses, one building each, photographed in 1964-65 while the committee compiled its architectural survey — nine of the ten published. *Here Today* itself is a lending-restricted lead in SOURCES.md; its research photographs are open.

coverage.remaining: Nothing in these 36 collections. What is left in the archive is SFP 130 (184 addressed), SFP 179 (151) and SFP 136 (30), all three blocked on #217, and the 128 collections that carry no addressed record at all.
coverage.note: Read every record in 36 collections: 7,261 unique catalogue records, of which 6,185 give no street number and are skipped and 888 are photographs of people that never reached the address test. 188 candidate addresses became 137 findings over 116 distinct addresses. 73 resolved, 33 unresolved, 31 rejected by hand. 45 published on 45 pages, 18 of them seeded by this run; 28 declined. A corpus-wide address pass over all 59,902 records finds no candidate in any unread collection outside these 36 and the three blocked on #217.
